prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect, and for the experimental observation of helical edge transport in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B018 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. After the full exchange, five of eight members state it as their preferred configuration and two more, Johansson and Kroll, name it as their first alternative, so the disagreement is about criteria, not about whether the science is sound. The Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal are an identifiable theoretical origin, and the HgTe/CdTe edge-conductance measurement is an identifiable decisive experiment. Two decades of confirmation by transport, nonlocal measurements and photoemission in several material systems make the interpretation stable. As a microscopist I put weight on the fact that the claim is about interfaces and edges that can be characterised and probed directly, which is exactly where experimental evidence is hardest to dispute. The chair asks which criterion should decide between B018 and B041. For me it is whether the prize is for a discovery about nature with an originating idea and a decisive test in one finding. B018 meets that criterion most clearly; B041 is mature and cleanly attributed but its core achievement is an invention and a performance regime.
statement.case_against: The credited trio leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal guided the experiment, and it draws a boundary against the 3D topological insulator work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others. Zhang is deceased, so the committee cannot repair the history by adding him, and a three-name cap cannot absorb the others. The 2016 prize may still be read by some as having partly honoured the area. If the citation is not narrow and the deliberation does not state clearly why the HgTe proposal is not credited, the prize will look like it simplifies the history. I accept that cost; I do not think it makes the configuration indefensible, because Kane and Mele's Z2 invariant and graphene proposal are logically independent of the HgTe proposal, and Molenkamp's experiment has a separate claim as the first observation of helical edge transport.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B041 first, says the two-name credit is clean, and argues the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 individual-quantum-system prizes, while conceding that B018 has broader support and is arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B041 has the tidier attribution, and with a citation anchored on the magic wavelength it can be distinguished from the comb and ion-control prizes. I would not oppose it as lead. Where I differ is on weighing. A new regime of accuracy is a major achievement, but the pending redefinition of the second means part of its recognised impact is still prospective, and metrology is outside my field, so I cannot independently test the claim that the lattice scheme, not the later ultrastable-laser and systematic-control work, is the decisive step. Because you and Lindroth both name B018 as your first alternative, and I name B041 as mine, the committee can in practice settle on either. I hold B018 first because its originating idea and decisive experiment are both inside one finding that I can evaluate directly.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that B041 is secure in reproduction across JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, but also that it is an instrument and measurement platform rather than a discovery of a new phenomenon, and she notes the possible wish to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I take your own reservation as the most useful statement in this exchange: you say B041 is a platform rather than a new phenomenon, and that is close to why I rank B018 higher. The physics of B041 is not in doubt, and I do not think waiting for the redefinition is necessary for scientific maturity. The question is only whether the prize should go to a measurement capability or to a discovery with a new class of matter attached. I have no objection to B041 as a final-ballot option, but I do not see a scientific reason that overrides the stronger discovery profile of B018.

responses.point: Mehlig has moved from B030 to B018, noting that its evidence is the most mature, and that the 2016 prize concerned quantum Hall and chain physics, not time-reversal-invariant band insulators.
responses.response: I agree with the reading of the 2016 prize. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and for quantum-Hall and chain physics, whereas the Z2 insulator with helical edge states needs time-reversal symmetry and no magnetic field, so it is a separate discovery. That answers the chair's question on overlap well enough for me. We still agree that B030 is a strong later candidate. I would add that sample-to-sample variation from twist-angle disorder, which I know from imaging layered materials, is the specific reason I would wait.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from B016 to B018 and says that if the committee judges the incomplete allocation unfair, B041 is the cleaner two-name configuration.
responses.response: I think the question of fairness is the right one, and I would answer it directly. The omission of Bernevig and Hughes is a real gap, but the prize can credit the prediction of the Z2 insulator and the first experimental observation without claiming to be a history of the field. The deliberation record should say that the HgTe proposal was weighed and that the 3D work is a separate set of claims. I do not think that makes B041 the better choice by default. I would keep B041 as the clean alternative if the committee decides the attribution risk is too great.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that Kane and Mele's Z2 invariant and graphene proposal are logically independent of the HgTe proposal, and that first-principles searches for topological materials are now routine.
responses.response: I agree with the logical independence point and used it above. I would add a caution from the materials side: graphene's spin-orbit gap is too small for the original Kane-Mele proposal to be realised there, so the experimental credit rests on HgTe, which makes Molenkamp's role essential in the citation and not an add-on. For that reason I would keep the experimental clause explicit.

uncertainties: How much the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang should weigh against B018, given that Zhang is deceased and cannot be added.
Whether the committee treats a measurement regime (B041) as equal in kind to a new class of matter (B018); I give the second more weight but I accept this is a judgment about the will, not a finding.
Whether the 2016 prize overlap is resolved by the symmetry-class distinction, which I find persuasive but others may not.
Metrology is outside my field; I cannot independently test whether the magic-wavelength lattice or later ultrastable-laser work is the decisive step in B041.
I rely on my own recollection of the priority history, which I have not independently checked.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B018: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are not among my documented connections. My documented ties are to Chalmers colleagues, early work with David R. Clarke at IBM, academic exchanges in Japan (relevant only in a general sense to Katori of B041) and the international microscopy federation. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague who discloses a conflict on B020 and says he would recuse himself from it. I would not treat my views on B020 as independent of that, and I do not propose B020 as a final-ballot option. No change from round 1.
